newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Manuel tells S.Africa bureaucrats to tighten belts. [CORRECTED 15:05 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Manuel tells S.Africa bureaucrats to tighten belts. [CORRECTED 15:05 GMT]

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel told public sector workers on Wednesday the government could not afford the higher wages they were demanding (corrects to delete implication that the government might even have to pay lower wages).
"We're concerned about the growing size of the wage bill as a percentage of that which we spend. Already it's at 49 percent of the non-interest expenditure of government," he told state radio.
"Clearly, there isn't room for it to increase."
Under terms agreed between the government and public sector unions last year, 6.5 billion rand ($1.3 billion) was allocated this fiscal year and the next to improve conditions of service.
In addition, money saved by laying off civil servants was added to the pot. Manuel put this figure at 323 million rand.
"That money is put on the table in the central bargaining chamber and the unions themselves determine how to apportion this," he said.
"The agreement that was signed last year allows the state as employer to revisit its offer if unforeseen circumstances arise which have severe negative implications for the economy...

"We don't have the resources available.... It is important that we take account of the difficulties we've lived through in the past year. The depreciation of the rand has cost this country fairly heavily."
Manuel said a wage agreement would have to take account of the cost of reducing the size of the public service, which has included payments to those volunteering to leave.

"You can't have salaries that are deemed to be market- related, at the same time pensions that are substantially higher than market-related...as well as a security of tenure that would see the state paying five years salary for every retrenchment," he said.

Referring to nine percent pay hikes sought by unions, Manuel said many workers in lower grades had already received increases of around 13 percent, adding: "Government has kept its side of the bargain."
Manuel noted the government had vowed not to exceed a four percent deficit this year.
"We've committed ourselves to lowering the portion of the budget that we spend on servicing state debt. It's incorrect in fiscal management to merely raise more and more debt," he added.
